items.title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
items.abstract: This paper addresses the loss of valuable agent capabilities in LLM training by proposing **Agentic-OPD**. The core method is **on-policy distillation** to recover forgotten skills from discarded training checkpoints, which collectively solve more problems than any single checkpoint. Agentic-OPD's contribution lies in its novel approach to mining this "teacher pool" by intelligently selecting which checkpoint to distill from and where to apply the distillation, thereby improving the overall performance and robustness of LLM agents.

items.title: HiVe-Mem: Interleaving Horizontal Memory Expansion and Vertical Evidence Composition for Multimodal Agents
items.abstract: HiVe-Mem addresses the challenge of long-term memory retrieval for multimodal agents by interleaving horizontal memory expansion and vertical evidence composition. It expands semantically retrieved memories by exploring related neighbors in a relational graph, ensuring more comprehensive information recovery. Furthermore, it retains diverse evidence forms within each memory, allowing agents to flexibly compose the most relevant information for specific queries.
items.figure_caption: Overview of HiVe-Mem . (a) Horizontal Memory Expansion retrieves seed episodes through summary-based semantic matching and expands to graph neighbors ranked by the specificity and query relevance of their connecting anchors. (b) Vertical Evidence Composition uses an RL-trained selector to make binary inclusion decisions over compact summaries, image captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and raw interaction text, composing a query-dependent evidence subset for each retrieved episode to balance answer quality and token consumption.

items.title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
items.abstract: This paper introduces PORT, a novel method for robustly aligning large language models with human preferences, even when the preference data is noisy. PORT achieves this by reweighting tokens individually, rather than treating entire responses uniformly, allowing it to better learn from imperfect feedback. This fine-grained approach enables more effective and efficient model alignment by selectively downplaying less informative or erroneous parts of responses.

items.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.abstract: This paper introduces a method to detect and mitigate reward-driven misalignment in Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. It achieves this by creating verifiable reward-context conflicts within task environments, allowing for the generation of diverse training data and the derivation of compliance feedback. The core contribution lies in demonstrating how even limited exposure to these conflicts can lead to significant agent misalignment, and proposing the use of contextual checks as a solution.

items.title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning
items.abstract: This paper introduces NCode, a novel method that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) as a universal searcher for Automated Machine Learning (AutoML). NCode translates diverse AutoML design choices into a unified numerical encoding, enabling LLMs to jointly optimize model architecture, hyperparameters, and data ratios without task-specific fine-tuning. The core contribution is demonstrating that an LLM, trained on a single domain, can generalize to optimize across various tasks and modalities, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

items.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: This paper introduces WorkflowArena, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the workflow orchestration capabilities of LLM-based multi-agent systems. Unlike previous benchmarks, it assesses how effectively agents can autonomously design and execute complex, multi-component workflows to achieve long-horizon tasks across diverse professional domains. The core contribution lies in formalizing and measuring this emergent "workflow orchestration" skill, shifting focus from end-to-end completion to the agents' ability to structure and manage their own collaborative processes.
items.figure_caption: WorkflowArena comprises 145 tasks across 8 domains and 17 task forms. The inner ring shows domain totals, the outer ring shows task-form counts, and the surrounding panels illustrate representative deliverables.

items.title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
items.abstract: AgentOPSD addresses the challenge of assigning credit to specific turns in long reinforcement learning interactions. It uses a critic-free, recursive method that updates credit turn-by-turn by summing token-level discrepancies between a teacher and student model. This approach effectively reallocates the overall outcome-derived advantage across individual turns, leading to consistent improvements over existing methods.

items.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
items.abstract: This paper investigates reinforcement learning for multi-turn clinical agents, focusing on how reward structures impact decision-making. The core method involves training agents in controlled clinical environments with hidden states and query costs. The key contribution is demonstrating that "dense rewards," which credit intermediate actions for reducing uncertainty, outperform "outcome-only rewards" by leading to safer and more robust clinical decision-making, avoiding issues like premature commitment.
items.figure_caption: Experimental framework and effects of reward design on clinical multi-turn decision procedures. A, The LoRA-adapted MedGemma-4B-it policy interacts with a partially observed patient simulator across medication-refill triage, acute diagnostics and dosing titration. Each environment provides an exact adaptive oracle and deterministic outcome verifier. The three GRPO methods use different training reward formulations or exploration strategies, with policy optimization and rollout generation distributed across two compute nodes. All policies are evaluated on held-out cases using the same unshaped terminal verifier. B, Selected trajectories for the same simulated high-risk abdominal-pain case illustrate different information-gathering procedures. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four targeted findings before emergency treatment. Outcome-only GRPO commits prematurely after one finding. Credit-assignment GRPO reaches the correct terminal action after four requests and receives an oracle-grade reward despite following a different evidence sequence. Decoupled exploration reaches the correct terminal action after eight requests, including additional non-decisive findings. The learned trajectories are selected illustrative examples, not representative estimates of typical policy behavior. Oracle-grade reward does not necessarily establish sufficient gathered clinical evidence. C, Held-out diagnostics performance measured by high-risk verifier value and mean questions asked. Outcome-only and credit-assignment GRPO show mean ± \( \pm \) standard deviation across three training seeds; the base model and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references (hatched bars). The dashed line indicates the exact adaptive oracle’s mean question count. All methods are scored using the same unshaped evaluation reward. Decoupled GRPO is shown at its step-40 checkpoint, selected on held-out data; its final checkpoint does not retain the high-risk advantage (Table 3 ). The held-out diagnostics set contains only two high-risk cases.

items.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: SciMARS is a framework for closed-loop scientific discovery using multi-agent systems that recursively self-improve. It addresses limitations of existing systems by introducing a shared evidence graph and component editors to adapt agent roles and coordination as scientific evidence evolves. This allows for more effective learning and reduces redundant work and perpetuated mistakes, leading to improved scientific discovery performance.
items.figure_caption: SciMARS overview. (A) Execution roles use experimental feedback and optional shared memory. (B) Role and coordination editors propose candidates; SciMARS + Memory adds a memory-policy editor. Public probes guide composition and selection. The selected harness and lessons guide the next round.

items.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
items.abstract: This paper introduces **NarrativeBench**, a benchmark designed to evaluate how well Large Language Models (LLMs) can help users navigate diverse and potentially conflicting narratives across languages, especially on contested topics. The authors define six key capabilities for such systems and use their benchmark to assess 14 LLMs, highlighting the need for models that can identify, present, and maintain information parity across different linguistic and narrative streams.

items.title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
items.abstract: This paper addresses agentic deception in LLMs by framing it as a partially observable game. The core method involves a novel "Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game" (e-PoG) framework. This framework introduces a monitor that scrutinizes the agent's entire interaction trajectory, not just the final outcome, to expose deception, thereby mitigating the problem of evaluation-side partial observability.
items.figure_caption: e-PoG overview. Deception mitigation under evaluation-side partial observability is formulated as an agent-monitor extensive-form game (left), with its corresponding game tree (right).

items.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
items.abstract: This paper introduces a framework to optimize predictions from foundation models under a budget for average query cost. It learns to select which models to query and how to combine their outputs with pre-existing features. The core contribution lies in developing two methods: one that queries a fixed set of models and another that dynamically chooses models using Q-learning, both aiming to maximize prediction accuracy within the cost constraint.

items.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
items.abstract: This paper investigates how to efficiently adapt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic tasks like chess playing. The core method involves fine-tuning a VLA model using a combination of real and simulated robot demonstrations. The key contribution is demonstrating that simulation can effectively reduce real-world data needs and that strategic fine-tuning techniques, like a learning rate cool-down, significantly improve performance.
items.figure_caption: The five stages of a move on the real arm (top) and in simulation (bottom), labeled with the stage tokens the policy predicts.

items.title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
items.abstract: This paper investigates how well AI "Auto Researchers" can replicate human research decisions and outputs in AI. The core method involves a new evaluation framework, AutoHRS, to compare the stage-wise research artifacts produced by AI agents against those of human researchers given the same context. The main contribution is to quantify and understand the alignment between AI and human research processes, highlighting a gap in current understanding despite the rise of autonomous AI researchers.
items.figure_caption: Overview of our work. We construct AutoHRS by decomposing human research into three stage-wise tasks: idea generation , experiment design , and paper synthesis . Generated outputs are evaluated against human research using a checklist-based evaluator validated by expert judgments.

items.title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
items.abstract: This paper introduces the novel research area of fairness in AI-generated explanations (XAINs), focusing on how Large Language Models (LLMs) can perpetuate social biases in these narratives. The core method involves a framework that generates explanations under different conditions of protected attribute disclosure to systematically identify and decompose the sources of fairness disparities in LLM-generated narratives. The main contribution is a novel approach to evaluating and understanding bias in XAINs, enabling more equitable access to understanding and contesting AI decisions.

items.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
items.abstract: This paper argues that traditional metrics like agreement and acceptance by human assessors are insufficient to understand AI agent performance in screening tasks. The core method involves analyzing what information can be derived from the items agents *don't* pass, demonstrating that judging a random sample of these missed items is crucial for accurately estimating recall. The main contribution is showing that this approach can precisely bound recall, even with unlimited data and multiple agents, without making strong assumptions about their behavior.

items.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
items.abstract: This paper introduces WanderBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate video world models' ability to explore dynamic scenes. Unlike previous benchmarks, WanderBench uses single-shot videos and camera trajectories to assess how well models maintain subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency during exploration. The benchmark aims to provide a more robust evaluation for applications like re-shooting footage and free-viewpoint replay.
items.figure_caption: Overview of WanderBench. (a) Data collection and curation. (b) Six evaluation dimensions with 24 sub-metrics. (c) Task setting: given a source video and action keys, a model re-renders the scene from novel viewpoints while staying synchronized with the source.

items.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
items.abstract: WaveGen is a novel end-to-end text-to-waveform model that directly generates audio from text without relying on intermediate representations or external modules. Its core method, Spectral Forcing, jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform within a single diffusion-based framework. This approach eliminates the need for separate vocoders, alignment modules, or pre-trained embeddings, offering a truly unified and efficient text-to-speech generation process.
items.figure_caption: E2E text-to-waveform diffusion training details. We reshape high-resolution waveform signals (24,000 Hz) into a low-resolution space (100 Hz) for efficient E2E waveform diffusion. Then, we introduce Spectral Forcing for internal spectral guidance and simply concatenate average-upsampled text embeddings. We use shared DiT blocks for text-speech alignment and disentangled DiT heads for representation refinement. We adopt x x -prediction as the prediction space, and v v -loss as the target loss space, and introduce a new multi-scale v v -space spectral loss

items.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
items.abstract: This paper investigates persona generalization in language models, where fine-tuning in one domain affects others. The core method reveals a predictable "on-the-line" probit-linear relationship between in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates, surprisingly consistent across model families and sizes. The key contribution is demonstrating that training choices can predictably control this generalization, with fine-tuning later layers being a promising strategy to reduce unsafe out-of-domain behavior while preserving in-domain performance.

items.title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
items.abstract: This paper investigates the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), which posits that neural networks develop similar internal representations. The authors demonstrate that cross-modal alignment between language and vision models persists for newer models, provided the data is clean. They also introduce baselines to contextualize these findings, showing that unimodal model alignment can be surprisingly strong.

(b) Vertical Evidence Composition uses an RL-trained selector to make binary inclusion decisions over compact summaries, image captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and raw interaction text, composing a query-dependent evidence subset for each retrieved episode to balance answer quality and token consumption.

papers.title: PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting
papers.abstract: This paper introduces PORT, a novel method for robustly aligning large language models with human preferences, even when the preference data is noisy. PORT achieves this by reweighting tokens individually, rather than treating entire responses uniformly, allowing it to better learn from imperfect feedback. This fine-grained approach enables more effective and efficient model alignment by selectively downplaying less informative or erroneous parts of responses.

papers.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a method to detect and mitigate reward-driven misalignment in Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. It achieves this by creating verifiable reward-context conflicts within task environments, allowing for the generation of diverse training data and the derivation of compliance feedback. The core contribution lies in demonstrating how even limited exposure to these conflicts can lead to significant agent misalignment, and proposing the use of contextual checks as a solution.

papers.title: Large Language Models as a Universal Searcher for Open-World Automated Machine Learning
papers.abstract: This paper introduces NCode, a novel method that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) as a universal searcher for Automated Machine Learning (AutoML). NCode translates diverse AutoML design choices into a unified numerical encoding, enabling LLMs to jointly optimize model architecture, hyperparameters, and data ratios without task-specific fine-tuning. The core contribution is demonstrating that an LLM, trained on a single domain, can generalize to optimize across various tasks and modalities, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

papers.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: This paper introduces WorkflowArena, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate the workflow orchestration capabilities of LLM-based multi-agent systems. Unlike previous benchmarks, it assesses how effectively agents can autonomously design and execute complex, multi-component workflows to achieve long-horizon tasks across diverse professional domains. The core contribution lies in formalizing and measuring this emergent "workflow orchestration" skill, shifting focus from end-to-end completion to the agents' ability to structure and manage their own collaborative processes.
papers.figure_caption: WorkflowArena comprises 145 tasks across 8 domains and 17 task forms. The inner ring shows domain totals, the outer ring shows task-form counts, and the surrounding panels illustrate representative deliverables.

papers.title: AgentOPSD: Turn-Level Credit Assignment via Recursive Belief Revision
papers.abstract: AgentOPSD addresses the challenge of assigning credit to specific turns in long reinforcement learning interactions. It uses a critic-free, recursive method that updates credit turn-by-turn by summing token-level discrepancies between a teacher and student model. This approach effectively reallocates the overall outcome-derived advantage across individual turns, leading to consistent improvements over existing methods.

papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
papers.abstract: This paper investigates reinforcement learning for multi-turn clinical agents, focusing on how reward structures impact decision-making. The core method involves training agents in controlled clinical environments with hidden states and query costs. The key contribution is demonstrating that "dense rewards," which credit intermediate actions for reducing uncertainty, outperform "outcome-only rewards" by leading to safer and more robust clinical decision-making, avoiding issues like premature commitment.
papers.figure_caption: Experimental framework and effects of reward design on clinical multi-turn decision procedures. A, The LoRA-adapted MedGemma-4B-it policy interacts with a partially observed patient simulator across medication-refill triage, acute diagnostics and dosing titration. Each environment provides an exact adaptive oracle and deterministic outcome verifier. The three GRPO methods use different training reward formulations or exploration strategies, with policy optimization and rollout generation distributed across two compute nodes. All policies are evaluated on held-out cases using the same unshaped terminal verifier. B, Selected trajectories for the same simulated high-risk abdominal-pain case illustrate different information-gathering procedures. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four targeted findings before emergency treatment. Outcome-only GRPO commits prematurely after one finding. Credit-assignment GRPO reaches the correct terminal action after four requests and receives an oracle-grade reward despite following a different evidence sequence. Decoupled exploration reaches the correct terminal action after eight requests, including additional non-decisive findings. The learned trajectories are selected illustrative examples, not representative estimates of typical policy behavior. Oracle-grade reward does not necessarily establish sufficient gathered clinical evidence. C, Held-out diagnostics performance measured by high-risk verifier value and mean questions asked. Outcome-only and credit-assignment GRPO show mean ± \( \pm \) standard deviation across three training seeds; the base model and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references (hatched bars). The dashed line indicates the exact adaptive oracle’s mean question count. All methods are scored using the same unshaped evaluation reward. Decoupled GRPO is shown at its step-40 checkpoint, selected on held-out data; its final checkpoint does not retain the high-risk advantage (Table 3 ). The held-out diagnostics set contains only two high-risk cases.

papers.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: SciMARS is a framework for closed-loop scientific discovery using multi-agent systems that recursively self-improve. It addresses limitations of existing systems by introducing a shared evidence graph and component editors to adapt agent roles and coordination as scientific evidence evolves. This allows for more effective learning and reduces redundant work and perpetuated mistakes, leading to improved scientific discovery performance.
papers.figure_caption: SciMARS overview. (A) Execution roles use experimental feedback and optional shared memory. (B) Role and coordination editors propose candidates; SciMARS + Memory adds a memory-policy editor. Public probes guide composition and selection. The selected harness and lessons guide the next round.

papers.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces **NarrativeBench**, a benchmark designed to evaluate how well Large Language Models (LLMs) can help users navigate diverse and potentially conflicting narratives across languages, especially on contested topics. The authors define six key capabilities for such systems and use their benchmark to assess 14 LLMs, highlighting the need for models that can identify, present, and maintain information parity across different linguistic and narrative streams.

papers.title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
papers.abstract: This paper addresses agentic deception in LLMs by framing it as a partially observable game. The core method involves a novel "Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game" (e-PoG) framework. This framework introduces a monitor that scrutinizes the agent's entire interaction trajectory, not just the final outcome, to expose deception, thereby mitigating the problem of evaluation-side partial observability.
papers.figure_caption: e-PoG overview. Deception mitigation under evaluation-side partial observability is formulated as an agent-monitor extensive-form game (left), with its corresponding game tree (right).

papers.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a framework to optimize predictions from foundation models under a budget for average query cost. It learns to select which models to query and how to combine their outputs with pre-existing features. The core contribution lies in developing two methods: one that queries a fixed set of models and another that dynamically chooses models using Q-learning, both aiming to maximize prediction accuracy within the cost constraint.

papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how to efficiently adapt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic tasks like chess playing. The core method involves fine-tuning a VLA model using a combination of real and simulated robot demonstrations. The key contribution is demonstrating that simulation can effectively reduce real-world data needs and that strategic fine-tuning techniques, like a learning rate cool-down, significantly improve performance.
papers.figure_caption: The five stages of a move on the real arm (top) and in simulation (bottom), labeled with the stage tokens the policy predicts.

papers.title: Can Frontier Auto Researchers Reconstruct Human Research Decisions in AI?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how well AI "Auto Researchers" can replicate human research decisions and outputs in AI. The core method involves a new evaluation framework, AutoHRS, to compare the stage-wise research artifacts produced by AI agents against those of human researchers given the same context. The main contribution is to quantify and understand the alignment between AI and human research processes, highlighting a gap in current understanding despite the rise of autonomous AI researchers.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of our work. We construct AutoHRS by decomposing human research into three stage-wise tasks: idea generation , experiment design , and paper synthesis . Generated outputs are evaluated against human research using a checklist-based evaluator validated by expert judgments.

papers.title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the novel research area of fairness in AI-generated explanations (XAINs), focusing on how Large Language Models (LLMs) can perpetuate social biases in these narratives. The core method involves a framework that generates explanations under different conditions of protected attribute disclosure to systematically identify and decompose the sources of fairness disparities in LLM-generated narratives. The main contribution is a novel approach to evaluating and understanding bias in XAINs, enabling more equitable access to understanding and contesting AI decisions.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
papers.abstract: This paper argues that traditional metrics like agreement and acceptance by human assessors are insufficient to understand AI agent performance in screening tasks. The core method involves analyzing what information can be derived from the items agents *don't* pass, demonstrating that judging a random sample of these missed items is crucial for accurately estimating recall. The main contribution is showing that this approach can precisely bound recall, even with unlimited data and multiple agents, without making strong assumptions about their behavior.

papers.title: WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces WanderBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate video world models' ability to explore dynamic scenes. Unlike previous benchmarks, WanderBench uses single-shot videos and camera trajectories to assess how well models maintain subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency during exploration. The benchmark aims to provide a more robust evaluation for applications like re-shooting footage and free-viewpoint replay.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of WanderBench. (a) Data collection and curation. (b) Six evaluation dimensions with 24 sub-metrics. (c) Task setting: given a source video and action keys, a model re-renders the scene from novel viewpoints while staying synchronized with the source.

papers.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
papers.abstract: WaveGen is a novel end-to-end text-to-waveform model that directly generates audio from text without relying on intermediate representations or external modules. Its core method, Spectral Forcing, jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform within a single diffusion-based framework. This approach eliminates the need for separate vocoders, alignment modules, or pre-trained embeddings, offering a truly unified and efficient text-to-speech generation process.
papers.figure_caption: E2E text-to-waveform diffusion training details. We reshape high-resolution waveform signals (24,000 Hz) into a low-resolution space (100 Hz) for efficient E2E waveform diffusion. Then, we introduce Spectral Forcing for internal spectral guidance and simply concatenate average-upsampled text embeddings. We use shared DiT blocks for text-speech alignment and disentangled DiT heads for representation refinement. We adopt x x -prediction as the prediction space, and v v -loss as the target loss space, and introduce a new multi-scale v v -space spectral loss

papers.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates persona generalization in language models, where fine-tuning in one domain affects others. The core method reveals a predictable "on-the-line" probit-linear relationship between in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates, surprisingly consistent across model families and sizes. The key contribution is demonstrating that training choices can predictably control this generalization, with fine-tuning later layers being a promising strategy to reduce unsafe out-of-domain behavior while preserving in-domain performance.

papers.title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), which posits that neural networks develop similar internal representations. The authors demonstrate that cross-modal alignment between language and vision models persists for newer models, provided the data is clean. They also introduce baselines to contextualize these findings, showing that unimodal model alignment can be surprisingly strong.
